title: "3. Design the Metaphor"
description: "Translate the technical model into a familiar world with an explicit technical-to-narrative mapping. Produce metaphor.md."

## Overview

A metaphor translates the technical model into a familiar world — a restaurant,
a theatre, an airport, a factory, a detective agency, or any setting where the
listener already has intuition about how things work. This lesson teaches you to
design a metaphor that is an **attempt at an isomorphism**: for every important
fact in the model there should be a counterpart in the story, and the story must
not introduce serious misconceptions.

You will produce a `metaphor.md` file with an explicit mapping table.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Translate a technical model into a metaphorical world with an explicit mapping
  table.
- Identify whether a metaphor is defensible: complete, isomorphic, navigable, and
  honest.
- Recognize and correct misconception injection — where the metaphor contradicts
  the model.
- Apply the "game the map" technique to test a metaphor against the key facts.

## Choosing a world

The metaphor must be a world the listener already understands intuitively. The
more familiar the world, the less explanation the metaphor itself needs and the
more energy you can spend on the technical content.

Common worlds:

| World | Good for modeling | Example mapping |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Restaurant | Request → fulfillment pipelines | Crossplane restaurant |
| Theatre | Role-based coordination | Actors, director, stage |
| Airport | Security, routing, gates | Requests flowing through checkpoints |
| Hotel | Reservation → service delivery | Guest requests processed by staff |
| Factory | Assembly, components, quality | Parts composed into products |
| Postal service | Addressing, routing, delivery | Messages flowing through a system |
| Detective agency | Investigation, evidence, resolution | Tracing problems to root cause |
| Orchestra | Coordination, roles, conductor | Many parts producing one output |

The world you choose must support the relationships in your concept. If your
system has a pipeline of hand-offs, a restaurant or factory works well. If it is
about coordination of many roles, an orchestra or theatre might be better.

## The mapping table

The `metaphor.md` file contains an explicit mapping table that connects every
entity in the technical model to its counterpart in the story world. This table
is the **contract** between `concept.md` and every other file in the pipeline.

Every character, scene, and sound effect must honor this table.

Here is the mapping from the Crossplane restaurant reference example:

| Crossplane (technical model) | Restaurant (metaphor) | Why it fits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| XRD (CompositeResourceDefinition) | Menu | Defines what can be requested. |
| Claim (XRC) | Order placed by a server | The developer's request for a specific dish. |
| Composite Resource (XR) | The order ticket | The concrete instance of the request. |
| Composition | Recipe | Says which components make up the dish. |
| Managed Resources (MR) | Prepared components | The individual parts of the dish. |
| Provider | Kitchen capability | How the real components actually get made. |
| Reconciliation | Chefs checking and perfecting | Desired state continuously matched to reality. |
| Crossplane engine | The restaurant's staff | The thing that composes and reconciles. |
| Developer | Customer | Requests the composite environment. |

## Attempt at an isomorphism

A defensible metaphor satisfies four properties:

- **Complete enough** — it covers the participating entities and their
  relationships. Every entity in the concept must appear in the mapping.
- **Isomorphic** — it adds no serious contradiction to the model. The mapping is
  one-to-one for the important facts.
- **Navigable** — a listener can map back from story to model. They can hear a
  character and know which technical entity it represents.
- **Playful but honest** — it is entertaining in service of understanding, never
  at its cost.

## Game the map

Before finalizing your metaphor, **game the map**: walk through each key fact
from your concept and check that the metaphor respects it.

For example, the Crossplane restaurant's key facts:

1. The developer asks for a *composite* environment, not individual pieces.
   → The customer orders a dish, not separate ingredients. Check.
2. The XRD defines *what can be requested*; the Composition defines *how it is
   built*.
   → The menu defines what can be ordered; the recipe says how it is made. Check.
3. The developer does **not** talk directly to providers.
   → The customer does not talk to the kitchen appliances. Check.

If any key fact fails the check, the metaphor must change — not the model.

## Avoiding misconceptions

The biggest risk in metaphor design is **misconception injection**: the story
introduces an idea that contradicts the real system.

For example, if the restaurant metaphor had the customer walking into the kitchen
and choosing their own ingredients, this would contradict the key fact that the
developer does not talk directly to providers. The customer must stay at the
table.

Be especially careful with:

- **Direction of communication** — does the story show the wrong entity talking
  to the wrong entity?
- **Timing** — does the story imply something happens at the wrong point in the
  process?
- **Scope** — does the story suggest an entity does more or less than it actually
  does?
